result.summary: Peleus wins the sea goddess Thetis by holding her fast through her changes, and she bears Achilles. Exiled for killing Phocus, he is welcomed by Ceyx, who tells how his brother Dædalion became a hawk after his daughter Chione's death. A wolf sent by Psamathe ravages Peleus's herds until Thetis wins pardon and the wolf is turned to marble.

scenes.title: Proteus's Prophecy and Jupiter's Retreat
scenes.summary: Proteus prophesies that Thetis's son will surpass his father. Jupiter, fearing this, gives her up to Peleus.
scenes.stakes: Jupiter fears being surpassed by a son of Thetis.

scenes.title: Peleus Seizes Thetis
scenes.summary: In a cave on the Hæmonian coast Peleus grasps Thetis as she changes shape. Proteus advises binding her, and she finally yields and bears Achilles.
scenes.stakes: Peleus risks losing Thetis, who escapes by changing shape.

scenes.title: Peleus Received by Ceyx
scenes.summary: Peleus arrives in Trachis, hides his crime and is welcomed by the grieving Ceyx.
scenes.stakes: Peleus needs refuge as an exile and conceals his guilt.

scenes.title: Dædalion and Chione
scenes.summary: Ceyx tells how Chione was violated by Mercury and Apollo and bore Autolycus and Philammon. Diana killed her for boasting, and the mad-with-grief Dædalion was made a hawk by Apollo.
scenes.stakes: Chione loses her life for slighting Diana; Dædalion seeks death in grief.

scenes.title: Antenor Reports the Wolf
scenes.summary: Antenor rushes in to report a monstrous wolf slaughtering Peleus's herds by the shore.
scenes.stakes: Peleus's herds and men are being destroyed.

scenes.title: Psamathe Appeased
scenes.summary: Peleus prays to Psamathe from a tower, Halcyone fears for him, and Thetis's plea turns the wolf to marble. Peleus then goes to Acastus for purification.
scenes.stakes: Peleus faces the sea goddess's wrath and loss of his herds.

alias_notes.explanation: Phœbus is a title of Apollo.
Mercury is called by his mother's name.
Proteus lived by the Carpathian sea.
Ceyx is called son of Lucifer, the morning star.

notable_quotes.reason: Thetis admits defeat after her transformations, ending the struggle.
Dædalion's transformation into a grieving, raging hawk.

analysis.text: Divine desire and human consequence run through the section: Thetis's forced marriage, Chione's rape and punishment, and Peleus's guilt all show mortals and gods entangled in violence.
Metamorphosis is both escape and punishment: Thetis changes shape to resist, Dædalion becomes a hawk, and the wolf becomes stone.

legacy.text: The union of Peleus and Thetis became the traditional background to the birth of Achilles and the Trojan War story in later literature.

fun_facts.text: Proteus, whose name gave English the word protean, is the sea god famed for changing form.

language_notes.text: Peleus and Telamon killed their half-brother Phocus; Peleus sought purification from Ceyx for the murder.
Peleus is Jupiter's grandson through Æacus, Jupiter's son. Jupiter hands over his own 'pretensions', his claim to Thetis, to Peleus.
Hæmonia is an old name for Thessaly in northern Greece, where Peleus lived.
'Carpathian prophet' is Proteus, the sea god, named for the Carpathian sea near Rhodes where he was said to dwell.
Titan here means the Sun (Phoebus), descended from the Titans. 'Hesperian main' is the western sea, where the sun sets.
A Nereid is one of the fifty sea-nymph daughters of Nereus; Thetis is one.
"Trachinian" means of Trachis, a city in Thessaly ruled by Ceyx. Peleus is fleeing there after killing his half-brother Phocus.
"Lucifer" is the morning star (Latin "light-bringer"), here personified as Ceyx's father, not the devil.
"Symbols of peace" are olive branches, held out by suppliants to show they come peacefully and ask for protection.
Peleus's grandfather was Jupiter, who was father of Æacus, so Ceyx honors him as of divine descent.
"He who summons forth Aurora" is Lucifer, the morning star, who rises before the dawn goddess and leaves the sky last.
Thisbe was a town in Boeotia famous for its doves, so "Thisbean doves" simply means doves.
"Son of Maia" is Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene; Phœbus is Apollo, whose famous oracle was at Delphi.
Apollo disguises himself as an old woman to approach Chione; the "delights before enjoyed in imagination" are those he had only anticipated.
"Make white out of black" describes Autolycus's skill at deceit, as a thief who could disguise stolen goods.
The son of Lucifer is Ceyx, king of Trachis, whom Peleus is visiting. His brother Daedalion was turned into a hawk, the wonder Ceyx has just told.
Trachinian means of Trachis, the city of Ceyx where Peleus is staying as an exile.
The Sun 'looking back' at what remains means it is noon: he can see as much of his course left behind as lies ahead.
Nereus and the Nereids are sea deities. The Nereids include Thetis, Peleus's wife, so the temple has a hidden personal link to him.
'Arms, I say' repeats the call for emphasis; the translator's bracket marks the speaker's urgent insistence.
Peleus's crime is the killing of his half-brother Phocus; the bereaved Nereid is Psamathe, Phocus's mother, who sent the wolf as vengeance.
Œtæan king: Ceyx, ruler of Trachis near Mount Œta. Peleus is his guest, since he is in exile.
The Divinity of the sea means Psamathe, a sea goddess. Peleus argues that only prayer, not weapons, can end her anger.
Azure describes the sea-blue goddess Psamathe, a Nereid (sea nymph).
Thetis, Peleus's wife, is also a Nereid and Psamathe's sister. This kinship explains why her plea succeeds where his failed.
Expiation of the murder means ritual purification from the blood-guilt of killing Phocus.

context_notes.text: Proteus was an old sea god who could foretell the future and change shape at will, which is why his advice on holding Thetis fits.
Dolphins were sea creatures associated with sea deities and nymphs, so Thetis riding one suits her as a sea goddess.
Achilles, son of Peleus and Thetis, became the greatest Greek warrior at Troy, fulfilling the prophecy that he would surpass his father.
Mercury's sleep-inducing wand is the caduceus, which he also used to lull Argus to sleep.
Diana, goddess of the hunt and chastity, was an archer and was quick to punish mortals who insulted her.
Parnassus was Apollo's mountain, sacred also to the Muses, which explains why the god is nearby to save Dædalion.
Nets drying on shore show a humble fishing coast; the temple is rustic, so the gods' worship is simple and local.
The wolf is sent by Psamathe, a Nereid, to avenge her son Phocus, whom Peleus and Telamon killed. The herdsman does not know this yet.
Coastal towers carried beacon fires to guide ships at night, so this tower serves as a lighthouse.
The Magnetes lived in Thessaly. Hæmonia is an old name for Thessaly, so Acastus is its king.

literary_notes.text: The narrator suddenly addresses Thetis directly as 'thou', adding intimacy and drama as the story turns to her fate.
Thetis's shape-changing into bird, tree and tiger repeats the Metamorphoses' central theme of transformation, here used as defence.
Proteus 'receives his own waves' as though the sea were welcoming him back, blending the god with his element.
The qualification about the killing of Phocus hints that Peleus's happiness will be troubled, leading into the next episodes of wrath and the wolf.
Chione is shot through the tongue, the very organ she used to boast, so the punishment fits the offense.
Dædalion's grief is compared to rocks that do not respond to the sea's murmurs, showing his inability to accept consolation.
The ox stung by hornets conveys Dædalion's frenzied, directionless anguish as he flees from the funeral pyre.
His seeming to have winged feet hints at his coming transformation into a bird.
The hawk keeps Dædalion's violent nature and grief, so its transformation preserves his character.
Antenor's doubled cry of Peleus's name heightens alarm and delays the news, building suspense.
Foam, clotted blood and eyes of red flame make the wolf vivid and terrifying, hinting at supernatural origin.
The wolf kills beyond hunger, from fury alone. This shows it is an instrument of divine vengeance, not a natural beast.
Blood reddening both shore and waves conveys the scale of the slaughter, with the lowing filling the fens.
Halcyone's half-arranged hair shows her panic and devotion, and her plea to save two lives in one shows her love.
The wolf is turned to stone in mid-act. This punishes its bloodlust and also ends the divine vengeance.
The wolf, once a terror, becomes a harmless monument. Its stony colour announces that the danger has passed.
